## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Palāsajātaka* (Ja 370) is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Blum 2013]. There are two stories entitled *Palāsa Jātaka* in the collection; the Pali term *palāsa* (*Butea monosperma* or *Butea frondosa*, commonly termed bastard-teak or dhāk) was translated by earlier Western translators as "Judas tree," while SuttaCentral adopts the rendering "The Parrot Tree" [SuttaCentral; Blum 2013].
The canonical prose setting places the narrative at Jetavana, where the Buddha addresses the monks on the rebuke of sin, warning that potential danger must be suspected: even a fault as small as a banyan shoot may prove fatal, just as the wise of old maintained vigilance against things open to suspicion [SuttaCentral]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a golden goose dwelling in the Himalayas who befriends the tree-spirit of a *palāsa* tree [McLeod 2010; Stanley et al. 2009; Fausböll 1883]. A bird that has eaten banyan fruit subsequently voids its excrement in a fork of the tree, giving rise to a banyan sapling [McLeod 2010; Fausböll 1883]. The goose warns the tree deity that the growing banyan parasite will eventually overwhelm and destroy the host tree and its shrine (*vimāna*), urging the deity to eradicate the shoot immediately [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. The warning is ignored, and the tree is ultimately destroyed [Anandajoti 2010]. The verse opens with the Bodhisatta addressing the tree: *Hamso palāsam avaca: nigrodho samma jāyati* ("The goose said to the Judas tree: 'A banyan, friend, is growing'") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883].
Regarding textual reuse and parallels, DharmaNexus finds eight shared segments between this canonical text and the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language matches, DharmaNexus automatically aligns the text with five passages in the Tibetan translation of Kṣemendra's *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* (D4155-2), although SuttaCentral lists no curated parallels [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the text across four languages [SuttaCentral].
